notes:
I've written notes for each verse from vv. 1–26. My budget for searches and page reads ran out before I could check every site, so a few gaps remain:
- **No notes from netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org.** I didn't reach them.
- **Nothing on Catholic or Orthodox teaching about divorce (vv. 9–12).** I didn't find it.
- **Nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings.** I didn't find any for these verses.
- **Some Enduring Word points have no tag.** David Guzik's full page cut off at v. 18. His points for vv. 2–16 are summarised from the full page and carry its URL without a citation tag; his later points come from the search summary.

---

**v. 1**
- Jesus is on his last journey towards Jerusalem. The commentary works out his route: east along Samaria's border, then across the Jordan into Peraea. Matthew adds that he healed as well as taught. (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- Precept Austin points out that Peraea was ruled by Herod Antipas. He had divorced his wife to marry Herodias, and John the Baptist was put to death over the question of these divorces! https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62149/

**v. 2**
- The question was a trap. Rabbi Shammai's followers allowed divorce only for moral defilement, while Rabbi Hillel's followers left it wholly up to the husband. The aim was to pit Jesus against one camp or the other. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- Dr. Constable suggests the Pharisees wanted Jesus to repeat John the Baptist's view of marriage. That might set him against Herod Antipas, since John had lost his head literally because of his views on marriage. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-10.html
- Guzik notes that Matthew's version adds "for just any reason," which shows what the real question was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/

**vv. 3–4**
- Moses permitted divorce; he did not command it. This cut against Hillel's school, which saw divorcing a wife who displeased you as a righteous duty. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/
- Matthew Henry: Moses allowed divorce for a time, but his account of creation gives a lasting reason that forbids it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_010.cfm
- Precept Austin quotes Swete: the "commandment" was really a set of rules meant to limit divorce and prevent abuse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62149/

**v. 5**
- The divorce certificate was a concession to sin. It added legal steps that could slow a divorce made in a moment of anger. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- Guzik: the hard heart could be either spouse's, the one who was unfaithful or the one unable to forgive. Quoting the scholar William Lane, he adds that the certificate partly protected the wife who was sent away. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/

**vv. 6–8**
- By quoting Genesis, Jesus went behind Moses to God's unchanging purpose. He neither approved of divorce nor contradicted Moses. (Coffman) https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/mark-10.html
- Pulpit Homiletics: marriage is part of how God made the world. Society recognises it but does not create it, so no human law can undo it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/mark/10.htm
- Gill: a married couple become "one body." There should be no separation until death, except in the case of adultery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-8.htm
- Guzik: Jesus moves the talk from divorce to marriage. "Joined" carries the idea of being glued, and the marriage bond should be stronger than the bond with parents. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/

**v. 9**
- Constable: it is wrong for people to break a bond God has made. Jesus sided with neither rabbinic school and upheld God's ideal of no divorce. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-10.html
- A commentator quoted on Precept Austin: Jesus doesn't claim every marriage is made in heaven, only that marriage itself is. His answer amounts to "No; not for any cause." https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62149/

**v. 10**
- The debate with the Pharisees was public, but this teaching was given privately indoors. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- Bengel: the disciples' repeated question drew out the same answer Jesus had already given the Pharisees. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-10.htm

**vv. 11–12, where readers differ on remarriage**
- *Strict reading:* Precept Austin says Jesus called remarriage after divorce adultery, whichever spouse sought the divorce. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62149/ The same page quotes a commentator who advises letting the words stand "in their uncompromising rigor as the ideal at which his followers ought to aim."
- *Reading Mark alongside the rest of Scripture:* Guzik (Enduring Word, the Pentecostal and charismatic site on your list) says divorce on biblical grounds gives a *full right* to remarry. Those grounds are adultery (Matthew 19:9) and being abandoned by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15). Being unhappy or incompatible is not grounds, though separation may be. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/
- *Matthew Poole:* Jesus here means divorces for trivial reasons. In those cases remarriage is adultery because the band of the former union holds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-10.htm
- *Pulpit (an Anglican work):* Jesus cancels the divorce certificate except for fornication. "Adultery against her" means against the wife who was put away and her rights. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- *v. 12:* Pulpit says this verse gives wives and husbands equal standing on divorce. Josephus shows that in practice they did not have equal rights at the time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm

**v. 13**
- Laying on hands meant a formal blessing. The disciples may have thought children were beneath so great a prophet. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- Barclay: the disciples weren't being rude. They simply wanted to protect Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/10-14.html

**v. 14: the clearest split between traditions (infant baptism)**
- *Lutheran:* the LCMS notes that the Greek word means babes in arms and says Infants can belong to the kingdom of God. It cites Pieper's hope that God may work faith in children of Christians who die unbaptised. https://www.lcms.org/about/beliefs/faqs/doctrine A 1517.org writer says Jesus shows little children can and do believe, and that in baptism we bring our children to him. https://www.1517.org/articles/let-the-little-children-come-to-me Luther rejected reading "children" here as only "the humble." https://resources.lcms.org/reading-study/concerning-rebaptism-for-christians/
- *Reformed:* Calvin says the passage shows Christ receives even those too young to know they need his grace. He uses it as a shield against the Anabaptists (the early opponents of infant baptism). https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom32/calcom32.ii.lxix.html
- *Anglican:* the Church Pulpit Commentary notes that the Church of England put this passage into its service for baptising infants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/mark-10.html Pulpit says the passage greatly encourages bringing children to baptism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- *Baptist:* Spurgeon's sermon "Children Brought to Christ, Not to the Font" argues the children weren't brought to be baptised. If the disciples had baptised infants, they would never have turned these parents away. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/children-brought-to-christ-not-to-the-font/ For him, coming to Christ means taking hold of him by faith, which is different from coming to a font. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/10-14.html
- *Churches of Christ (Coffman):* Here is no allusion to baptism. In his view, belonging to the kingdom requires understanding and personal faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/10-14.html
- *Catholic:* catholic.com uses this verse to support the Catechism's hope that God provides a way of salvation for infants who die unbaptised. Baptism is still the ordinary means. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/let-the-children-come-to-me

**v. 15**
- Guzik: the point isn't children's innocence but that they simply receive. They don't feel they must earn what they're given. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/
- Pulpit: adults must drop ambition and copy children's simplicity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm

**v. 16**
- Jesus embraced each child, then laid his hand on its head and blessed it. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- Guzik: the Greek verb means to bless fervently. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/

**v. 17**
- Gill: calling eternal life an "inheritance" should have taught the man it is a free gift, not earned by works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-17.htm
- Constable: the man was earnest and respectful but he viewed eternal life as something one must earn. Mark sets him against the childlike receiving of vv. 13–16. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-10.html

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: Jesus is lifting the man to a higher faith, in effect saying "If you call me good, believe that I am God". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- Adrian Rogers (Baptist) on Precept Austin: Jesus is showing the young man that he himself—the young man—is not good. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-10-commentary

**v. 19**
- Jesus stresses the commandments about loving one's neighbour, because love of God shows itself in love of others. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm

**v. 20**
- Guzik: keeping these commandments was possible as they were usually interpreted, but *impossible* according to the true meaning of God for these commandments. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/
- Precept Austin cites Luther's maxim: preach law to the proud and grace to the humble. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-10-commentary

**v. 21**
- only Mark records that Jesus loved him. He loved him enough to tell him the truth. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-10-commentary
- Pulpit: the order to sell everything was a personal instruction aimed at this man's covetousness, not a command for everyone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- Guzik: the man's problem was trusting wealth rather than God, and he wanted salvation through doing, not receiving. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/

**v. 22**
- Constable: this is the only time in the Gospels when someone called to follow Jesus did not do so. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-10.html
- Matthew Henry: Jesus didn't soften his words or call the man back. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_010.cfm

**v. 23**
- Why riches are dangerous: they tempt people to pile them up, tie the soul to earth, and feed pride. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/10.htm
- Coffman: rich people can be saved, but wealth makes the needed decisions harder. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/mark-10.html
- Guzik: compared with this ruler, most of us today are rich. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/

**v. 24**
- Barnes: "Children" is a term of affection, perhaps also a mild rebuke for slowness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-25.htm
- R.C. Sproul (Reformed) reads the verse with the wording "how hard it is for those who trust in riches" and says Jesus' repetition clarifies the warning. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-eye-needle

**v. 25: the "needle gate" debate**
- *Most commentators:* this is deliberate overstatement to show something impossible. John MacArthur's site (gty.org) says there is no evidence that such a gate ever existed. The point is that saving yourself is as impossible as threading a camel through a needle. https://www.gty.org/blogs/B150914/what-is-the-eye-of-a-needle Sproul says the gate story is a legend from about the ninth century. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-eye-needle
- *Early church writers:* Origen, Jerome and Cyril of Alexandria took the saying as absolute impossibility. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_does_Jesus_mention_camel_needle.htm
- *The popular "gate" teaching:* Chuck Smith described a small night-time side gate where a camel had to be unloaded and squeezed through. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/10-25.html Spurgeon's sermon page also carries Canon Farrar's report of travellers who had heard small doorways called "the needle's eye." https://biblehub.com/sermons/mark/10-25.htm
- *"Cable" instead of "camel":* some have suggested this reading. Wuest replies that the Greek means a sewing needle, not a gate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/10-25.html

**v. 26**
- The disciples assumed wealth was a sign of God's blessing, so Jesus' words overturned what they expected. https://biblehub.com/mark/10-25.htm
- The camel saying is the overstatement that explains why they were so astonished. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_does_Jesus_mention_camel_needle.htm
